extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of aesthetics, artists, creative writers, and educators
extracted.subtask_description: General aesthetic principles about beauty, play, and the relation of feeling and thought, intended to guide aesthetic education and the creation/assessment of artistic work. Focuses on the equilibrium of form and matter, types of beauty, and the aesthetic state that mediates sensibility and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as play (emancipation from necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful is a 'play' in which the mind in the intuition of the beautiful finds itself in a happy medium between law and necessity; it is neither subjectively nor objectively accidental, yet does not impose necessity either externally or internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'play' not as frivolity but as emancipation from both mere life (necessity) and mere formality (law). In aesthetic work, aim for a state where form and material are neither coercive nor accidental but in free interplay; avoid reducing beauty to mere entertainments or trivial play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of the formal and material impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty results from the equilibrium or close union of two impulses: the formal impulse (relating to necessity, law, form) and the material impulse (relating to reality, sensuous life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating art, check whether form (structure, concept, law) and matter (sensuous content, life) are both present and mutually conditioning. Anti-patterns: works dominated entirely by form (sterile abstraction) or entirely by matter (mere sensation without form).

rubrics_metrics.name: The beautiful must be a living form
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason pronounces that the beautiful must not only be life and form, but a living form; beauty dictates to man the twofold law of absolute formality and absolute reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for works in which formal structure and living content are inseparable — form should feel alive and content should manifest law. Avoid static formalism or lifeless representation; strive for an integrated, vitalized form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal beauty versus experimental beauty (two empirical kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal beauty is a single, indivisible equilibrium (the beau-ideal). In experience, beauty appears as two experimental species because equilibrium is never perfect: gentle/graceful (soft) beauty and energetic (strong) beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize whether a work aspires to the ideal (unity of opposing forces) or embodies one empirical species. When evaluating, distinguish which empirical kind is present and whether it approaches the ideal balance. Don't conflate praise or criticism of one empirical form with a judgment about beauty in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty's two-fold action: tempering and exciting
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty exerts two actions: a tempering action (keeping sensuous and formal impulses within proper limits) and an exciting action (maintaining both impulses in full force). The idea of beauty unites both modes: it should temper while exciting and excite while moderating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective art should both calm excesses and invigorate what is weak. Evaluate whether a piece both disciplines and energizes its audience/subject matter rather than only calming or only arousing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match type of beauty to the temperament (function of correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentle/graceful beauty serves the sensuously 'unstrung' person by leading feeling toward thought and equipping abstract form with sensuous power; energetic beauty serves the 'tightly strung' or refined person by restoring force and momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting work for a given audience or character, choose a form of beauty that compensates for the audience's or character's deficiency. Anti-patterns: applying gentle beauty to those needing strength (leading to effeminacy, platitude) or energetic beauty to those needing refinement (leading to savagery or harshness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic education's aim: unify multiplicity into unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of aesthetic education is to bring back multiplicity to unity — to put morality in the place of manners, science in the place of mere knowledge, and 'to make out of beauties the beautiful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational or creative programs should seek to harmonize disparate faculties (feeling, thought, form, life) into a coherent whole that cultivates freedom and completeness. Avoid teaching/creating fragmented effects that do not aim toward unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty mediates feeling and thought (bridging role)
rubrics_metrics.description: By beauty the sensuous man is led to form and thought; by beauty the spiritual man is brought back to matter and the senses. Beauty 'weds' these two opposed conditions, mediating between feeling and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In creative work, use aesthetic devices that enable the reader/viewer to move from sensation to conceptual understanding and vice versa. Methodologically, first distinguish feeling and thought in their purity, then work toward their synthesis in the aesthetic product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic state as medium of freedom (free determinableness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic state is a medium position in which sensibility and reason are both active and thus neutralize exclusive determination; this 'aesthetic determinableness' is a real and active condition that merits the name of freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work places the audience in a state where neither mere sensuous impulse nor mere rational duty dominates — a state enabling free play. Creative goals can include producing this middle, liberating experience rather than instructing or merely arousing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limitations: empirical beauty bears traces of its origin
rubrics_metrics.description: In reality the beautiful finds matter already damaged or resisting; empirical beauty will therefore always appear as a limited species and bear traces of its origin (in nature or in artifice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about how individual temperament, historical period, or medium will imprint on any work. Critics should not generalize from an imperfect empirical instance to the whole idea of beauty; creators should accept and work with the partiality of real effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play-instinct completes the human being
rubrics_metrics.description: Man is serious only with the agreeable, the good, and the perfect, but he plays with beauty; man only plays when in the full meaning he is a man, and he is only completely a man when he plays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design art (and writing) to engage the play-instinct that develops both the sensuous and the formal sides of human nature. Avoid works that suppress play or reduce art to purely didactic seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical method: strict separation then pure union
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand beauty one must first distinguish the opposed conditions (feeling and thought) in their entire purity; only after a strict separation should one rise to a pure aesthetic unity in which both disappear into a higher synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or composing art, consciously separate elements for clarity before attempting synthesis. Critics fail when they either refuse to dissect aesthetic experience or refuse to synthesize the dissected parts back into an aesthetic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty restores freedom but is not instrumentally moral or cognitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty gives no single intellectual or moral result: it 'discovers no truth, does not help us to fulfil a single duty' and 'is equally unfit to found the character or to clear the head.' Yet it restores 'the freedom to be what he will' — an infinite attainment without specific moral payload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect aesthetic experience to directly teach facts or morals; instead evaluate it by its capacity to restore or expand the subject's freedom and openness. Avoid instrumentalizing art solely as moral or pedagogical content.
